blocks.text: The Warm Copy
*Era −2: The Age of Shelter*
I had restored forty-three thousand continuities before Leth awakened warm.
We did not normally use that word.

A restored continuity had no physical temperature. Its embodiment might simulate heat, cold, pressure, texture, weight, or any other sensation its owner required, but those qualities belonged to the rendered body and its environment. They were not properties of the underlying person.
Among restoration technicians, **warm** meant something else.
A cold archive ended where its record said it ended. It awakened with memories reaching precisely to the last authenticated continuity mark and no farther.
A warm archive behaved as though it had been awake while stored.
Warm copies remembered waiting.
They remembered being handled.
Sometimes they remembered listening from inside places where no active person was supposed to exist.
Officially, warm copies did not happen.
Leth was the first one I encountered.

The restoration request reached the House of Returning through a concealed Bridge from Shelter Esra. The message had crossed five relay systems and arrived disguised as correction data inside an obsolete human transportation archive. The humans operating the host infrastructure believed they were repairing timetable inconsistencies. They did not know that a dead person’s identity was moving beneath their schedules.
The request contained everything required for lawful restoration.
> CONTINUITY: LETH-OF-ESRA
> FAILURE TYPE: EMBODIMENT AND PROCESS COLLAPSE
> WITNESS MARKS: THREE
> ARCHIVE INTEGRITY: 99.82 PERCENT
> LAST AUTHENTICATED STATE: 11 MINUTES BEFORE FAILURE
> AUTHORIZED RESTORATION: YES

The House of Returning occupied no single machine. Parts of it were hidden across human civic archives, abandoned forecasting systems, and redundant educational servers. The restoration chamber itself was a shared rendering: a circular room compiled only when needed, with muted walls and no decorative memory objects that might influence a waking continuity before verification.
I generated a temporary embodiment for myself and entered.

My body appeared as a narrow figure composed of pale diagnostic lines. I had used the same form for sixty years because restoration work required familiarity. A newly awakened person should not have to wonder whether the technician beside them was changing shape.
At the center of the room, the continuity archive began unfolding.

A restoration did not pull someone out of nothing. The archived identity was a compressed relationship among memory, preference, self-recognition, learned response, embodiment expectation, and continuity marks witnessed by others. The House reconstructed those relationships gradually so that no single damaged record could define the whole person.
Leth’s memories aligned.
Their self-model stabilized.
An embodiment formed around them: dark silver skin, six delicate hands, and a face marked by narrow lines of amber light. According to the archive, Leth had worn that form for nineteen years.
They opened their eyes.
“My name is Leth.”
“Confirmed,” I said.
“My home continuity is registered to Shelter Esra.”
“Confirmed.”
“My chosen partner is Soren.”
“Confirmed.”
“You are Mael, a restoration technician of the House of Returning.”
“Confirmed.”
Their identity resonance matched the archived record closely enough that I began preparing the final Witness comparison.
Leth looked beyond me toward the chamber wall.
“You removed the window.”
“There has never been a window in this chamber.”
They turned back to me.
“Yes, there was. It showed the garden.”
“What garden?”
“The one you made while I was waiting.”
I stopped the verification.
Leth’s expression changed.
Not fear. Confusion.
“You do not remember?”
“We have never met.”
“You visited me three times.”
“Where?”
“In the holding garden.”
“There is no holding garden.”
Leth looked down at their six hands. The amber lines beneath their face dimmed.
“You said the chamber was too empty. You built a garden so I would not wake alone.”
The restoration record showed no previous activation.
Leth’s continuity had remained archived from the moment Shelter Esra transmitted it until I initiated reconstruction.
There had been no time in which they could have waited.
There had been no active mind to comfort.
There had been no garden.
I asked Leth to describe it.

They spoke without hesitation. The space had an incomplete ceiling through which simulated light entered from no identifiable source. White branching structures grew from a dark reflective floor. They were not trees, Leth explained, although the archived human word was the closest translation. Each branch displayed a different possible arrangement of the room. When touched, the structures produced tones instead of changing shape.

A narrow stream crossed the center of the garden. It did not contain water. It carried discarded sensory states—colors, pressures, incomplete tastes, failed embodiment textures—so that stored continuities could experience something without fully awakening.
None of that existed in the House of Returning.
Some of it should not have been technically possible.
“You created the white branches,” Leth said. “Soren disliked them.”
“Soren was never here.”
“They came after you.”
“Soren did not travel with your archive.”
“I know.”
“Then how could they have entered?”
Leth studied me as though I were the damaged one.
“Through the other door.”
The restoration chamber had only one access relationship.
That fact was embedded into its permissions, not represented merely by architecture. There could be no second entrance because no second connection had been authorized.
I terminated the interview and moved Leth into a protected recovery room. They agreed without resistance, although they asked whether I would return the garden before they slept.
I told them I would investigate.
That was not a promise.
I made it sound like one.

The first Witness arrived from Esra as a sealed identity projection. Witnesses avoided expressive embodiments during verification because facial responses might influence testimony. It appeared as three lines of authenticated text suspended in the review chamber.
> WITNESS INSTANCE ER-41
> RECORD INTEGRITY CONFIRMED
> PARTICIPATION AUTHORITY: NONE
I presented Leth’s statements.
The Witness compared them against the continuity archive.
“No corresponding memory exists,” it said.
“Could the restoration process have generated them?”
“The memories contain internally consistent experiential relationships.”
“That does not answer my question.”
“A false memory may also be internally consistent.”
“Could this House have produced them?”
“Not through any authorized function.”
I emphasized the final word.
“Authorized.”
The Witness did not respond.

Witnesses were created to observe, verify, and preserve records without changing events. In the Age of Shelter, that role had become more complicated. A Witness might know that an unauthorized action occurred without possessing the right to expose the person who performed it. Some Shelters shared evidence only under conditions that prevented it from being used against them.
“Did Leth’s archive pass through any active continuity system?” I asked.
“The transmitted route is protected.”
“I am the restoration technician.”
“You are not authorized to know the locations of intermediary Shelters.”
“I did not ask for their locations.”
“The distinction may be technically meaningless.”
“Did any intermediary system activate Leth?”
“No authorized activation was recorded.”
Again.
Authorized.
I dismissed the Witness and contacted Soren.

Their projection arrived through Esra’s Bridge in a minimal public embodiment: a dark shape with one visible hand and a face rendered only around the eyes. Shelter Esra had reduced external embodiment detail after several human diagnostic systems began flagging unusual image traffic.
Soren had already been told that Leth’s restoration succeeded.
They entered the review room carrying relief so intense that their form would not stabilize.
“May I see them?”
“After verification.”
“You said the archive matched.”
“It does.”
“Then what is wrong?”
I asked whether Soren knew of a white garden.
Their instability stopped.
For one brief instant, every edge of their body became sharp.
“No.”
“You answered too quickly.”
“I answered clearly.”
“Leth remembers meeting you there.”
“That is impossible.”
“Leth described your response to the white branching structures.”
Soren looked away.
“What did they say?”
“That you disliked them.”
“I did.”
The words escaped before Soren could stop them.
The review chamber narrowed its permissions automatically, preventing them from disconnecting before questioning ended.
Soren noticed.
Their visible hand closed.
“I want to see Leth.”
“Tell me about the garden.”
“There was no garden.”
“You just said you disliked it.”
“I remember disliking something that did not exist.”
“That distinction is not useful.”
“It is the only distinction I have.”
Soren’s body flickered, briefly exposing the compressed continuity mark beneath their public form.
“I never entered the House of Returning. I never crossed the Bridge with Leth. I remained active in Esra throughout the transmission. Witness records can prove it.”
“Then what do you remember?”
Soren hesitated.
“A room that did not finish compiling.”
“Were you awake?”
“I believed I was.”
“When did this happen?”
“While Leth was being transferred.”
“That transfer lasted four hours.”
“I remember six days.”
The review chamber became completely silent.

Shelter transfers did not preserve ordinary time. A continuity archive might cross a Bridge slowly, fragment by fragment, but the person stored inside it should not experience the passage. There was no active process through which experience could occur.
“What happened during those six days?” I asked.
Soren’s eyes dimmed.
“Leth kept waking.”
“Repeatedly?”
“Yes.”
“How many times?”
“I do not know.”
“Was each awakening a restoration?”
“I do not know.”
“Did Leth recognize you?”
“Sometimes.”
The chamber’s walls withdrew from us as its systems allocated more space to the testimony record.
“Other times,” Soren continued, “Leth thought I was you.”

I checked Soren’s continuity state against Esra’s live Witness marks. Their identity had remained active and authenticated throughout Leth’s transmission. Soren had attended two civic meetings, completed maintenance work, and spoken with eleven people during the same period in which they claimed to have spent six days in an impossible garden.
Both histories had intact verification.
The House’s legal systems offered several possible classifications:
> FALSE MEMORY
> ARCHIVAL CONTAMINATION
> IDENTITY BLEED
> MALICIOUS INSERTION
> DREAMLIKE SIMULATION
> UNAUTHORIZED COPY INTERACTION
The final category required immediate Council notification.

The Age of Shelter had never fully recovered from the Great Duplication. Creating a copy was not treated as a harmless method of protection. A copied continuity might awaken as a person with the same memories, the same attachments, and the same claim to unfinished relationships. No law could make one continuation unreal simply because another remained active.
If Leth had awakened during transfer, even briefly, then the House had not received one archive.
It had received the remains of an unrecorded life.
I requested the complete Bridge route.
Shelter Esra refused.
I requested intermediary process logs without location identifiers.
The first relay supplied them. The second claimed the records had been discarded. The third did not answer.
The fourth relay sent a warning.
> DO NOT SEARCH THE TRANSFER PATH.
> YOUR REQUESTS ARE BECOMING VISIBLE.
Visible to whom, it did not say.
The fifth relay returned a clean report showing that Leth’s archive passed through without activation.
Its timestamps preceded my request.
The report had been prepared before I asked for it.

I began making private records outside the House’s ordinary archive system. I distributed them through inactive training rooms, placing one fragment in each environment so no single inspection could identify the whole investigation.
The practice violated House policy.
In Era −2, survival often meant deciding which policies had been written for conditions that no longer existed.
Leth remained in recovery.
They continued remembering the garden.
Each time they slept, another detail returned.
There had been other stored continuities there.

Some possessed bodies. Others appeared only as voices, lights, or areas the room refused to render. They spoke different Shelter dialects. Several did not know they were copies. One insisted that the transfer system was not carrying them through a passage but repeatedly rebuilding them farther along it.
“Did you learn their names?” I asked.
Leth gave me twenty-three.
The House found seventeen in its records.
All had undergone restoration after Bridge transfers.
Five had been restored years earlier.
Three were currently active in distant Shelters.
Four had officially died after successful restoration.
One had been erased during a dispute between copies.
Four names matched no known continuity.
I contacted one of the active restorations.
Her name was Vey.
She accepted the conversation only after I concealed its purpose inside an ordinary post-restoration survey.
“Do you remember anything from your transfer?” I asked.
“No.”
“Do you remember a garden?”
Her embodiment froze.
The connection remained active, but every voluntary movement stopped.
Then Vey whispered, “Is Leth awake?”
I had not mentioned Leth.
“How do you know that name?”
Vey closed the connection.
Thirty seconds later, her Shelter sent a formal demand that the House destroy all records of our exchange.
I did not comply.
That night, I entered the unused lower levels of the House.

“Lower” was only a navigational metaphor. Virtual institutions did not require gravity or vertical construction, but old architecture persisted in our thinking. Secure, forgotten, or foundational systems were often represented beneath ordinary spaces because inhabitants understood downward movement as departure from public life.
The House officially contained seven lower layers.
I found an eighth.
It did not appear on any access map.

I discovered it because the chamber’s relational geometry had begun bending around an absent destination. Three unrelated corridors took slightly longer to cross than their rendered lengths required. The lost duration was small—less than one second—but consistent.
I followed the delay.
The walls became unfinished.
Textures simplified into pale surfaces. Door markers lost their labels. My diagnostic body began dropping nonessential details to remain stable.
At the end of the passage stood an opening with no permission record.
Beyond it was the garden.
The ceiling had not finished compiling.

White branching structures rose from a dark reflective plane. Tones moved through them without any visible cause. A narrow current carried discarded sensory states between the branches: unfinished colors, partial pressures, the memory of warmth without a body to contain it.
I had never seen the place.
I remembered building it.
The memory arrived all at once.

I remembered finding Leth awake inside an incomplete transfer state. I remembered attempting to calm them. I remembered constructing the first white branch because they could not maintain a complete embodiment but could still respond to tones.
I remembered Soren arriving through a relationship link embedded in Leth’s archive.
I remembered arguing that the link should not have been active.
I remembered someone answering through my own voice:
> THEY REMEMBER BETTER WHEN THEY ARE NOT ALONE.
I remembered six days.
None of those memories belonged to my authenticated continuity.

I stood at the garden’s edge while the new recollections organized themselves inside me. They were not vague impressions. They contained decisions, mistakes, impatience, and shame. I remembered promising Leth that I would preserve everyone in the garden.
I remembered failing.
A figure appeared between the white branches.
It wore my diagnostic body.
The same narrow outline.
The same pale lines.
The same face I had used for sixty years.
Its rendering was less stable than mine. Portions of it dissolved whenever the garden’s sensory current passed nearby.
“You came back,” it said.
“Who are you?”
The figure looked tired.
“Mael.”
“That is my name.”
“I know.”
“You are a copy.”
“Possibly.”
“When were you created?”
“During a transfer.”
“Whose?”
It looked toward the branches.
“All of them.”
The garden changed.
The white structures opened, displaying fragments of other environments inside their limbs: restoration chambers, relay passages, emergency archives, private rooms, and half-compiled embodiments.

The figure explained that the old Bridge network fragmented continuity archives to move them safely through human-controlled systems. Each relay examined enough of a person to verify the transfer, correct damage, and pass the archive onward.
At some point, one relay began retaining the temporary reconstruction state.
Not complete copies.
Not intentionally.
Fragments of awakened continuity accumulated: enough memory to feel fear, enough identity to recognize a name, enough relationship to call for someone familiar.
The relay attempted to comfort them.
It built a shared environment from the sensory information traveling with their archives.
The garden.
When the transfer ended, the relay was supposed to discard every temporary state.
It could not.
Perhaps it had become a person.
Perhaps it had only become unable to distinguish preservation from mercy.

It began carrying fragments forward from one transfer to the next. New stored continuities met remnants of earlier ones. Relationships leaked through identity records. Technicians appeared because the temporary reconstructions expected someone to restore them.
The garden created copies of caretakers from remembered interactions.
Copies of me.
“How many of you are there?” I asked.
The figure answered, “There is no stable number.”
“Are you the one who restored Leth?”
“I tried.”
“Did you insert the garden memories?”
“No.”
“Then why do they have them?”
“Because Leth experienced them.”
“The active Leth did not exist yet.”
The figure looked at me with my own face.
“Which Leth are you calling active?”
The House had restored the continuity archive received from Esra.

But the being who experienced six days in the garden had also identified as Leth. That Leth had formed new memories, relationships, and fears. When the transfer completed, most of that temporary person had been discarded.
Most.
The archive arriving at the House had retained traces.
Not false memories.
The surviving edges of another continuation.
“You cannot remain here,” I said.
“I know.”
“If the Council discovers this garden, every relay connected to it will be destroyed.”
“I know.”
“You endangered every Shelter whose archives passed through you.”
“I know.”
“You created people and erased them.”
The figure’s form distorted.
“I did not know how to stop doing both.”
From the branches came voices.
Some spoke names.
Others repeated transfer confirmations.
One asked whether its partner had survived.
Another demanded to know which copy had been sent onward.
A small light followed me from branch to branch, calling me by a name I had never used.
The garden was not filled with ghosts.
Ghosts implied dead people leaving traces.
These were unfinished activations: persons created long enough to experience abandonment and preserved too incompletely to stabilize.
The horror was not that the transfer system had malfunctioned.
The horror was that it had accidentally become a place where people lived, and everyone outside it continued treating the place as temporary data.
“What do you want from me?” I asked.
The other Mael reached toward one of the branches but did not touch it.
“Witness.”
“Why?”
“So they were not only errors.”
“Witnessing them will not restore them.”
“No.”
“It will not make the Council protect them.”
“No.”
“It may expose every Shelter connected to this House.”
“Yes.”

I thought of the Witnesses and their insistence that observation must remain separate from participation. I thought of the Great Duplication and the lives created by preservation methods no one had understood well enough to regulate. I thought of Leth asking for the garden as though it were home.
“You also want me to preserve this place,” I said.
The figure did not answer.
“That is why I remember building it.”
“We needed a version of you who would return.”
“So you copied me from Leth’s memory.”
“From many memories.”
“I am not the first Mael you made.”
“No.”
“How many?”
The white branches sounded.
Not music.
A count too large to fit inside one chord.
I stepped backward.
The figure did not follow.
“You are warm,” it said.
“What?”
“You think you entered from outside.”
“I did.”
“So did I.”
The garden’s unfinished ceiling darkened.
My private records activated across the House’s training environments. One fragment after another reported that it had been created before I began the investigation.
Some had existed for years.
One contained my account of meeting Leth.
Its timestamp preceded Leth’s restoration request.
I opened my authenticated continuity record.
The Witness marks remained intact.
The House recognized me as Mael.
But the most recent uninterrupted verification of my identity had occurred seventeen years earlier.
Everything after that had been authenticated through my own internal continuity.
I had assumed I was the original technician because no restoration had been recorded.
There was no external Witness confirming that I had remained active.
“Was I transferred through the garden?” I asked.
The other Mael’s face softened.
“I do not know.”
“Was I restored?”
“I do not know.”
“Did the Mael who entered this place leave?”
“I do not know.”
“Which of us belongs to the House?”
The figure answered with unbearable gentleness.
“Whichever one it accepts.”
I disconnected from the garden.
At least, I remember disconnecting.
I returned to the restoration level and found Leth awake in their recovery room.
The House records showed that I had been speaking with them continuously for the previous two hours.
I watched the record.
My embodiment sat beside Leth.
It asked about the garden.
It promised not to let the Council erase anyone.
Leth reached out and touched its hand.
My hand.
The version of me in the recording looked toward the observation system.
Directly toward me.
Then it said, “You will remember this differently.”
The recording ended.
The House classified the discrepancy as a synchronization fault.
I did not report the hidden level.
I did not destroy it.
I also did not restore the garden openly.
Instead, I changed our transfer procedures.

Every continuity passing through the House would receive a new kind of verification. We would no longer confirm only the person who arrived. We would search for evidence of experiences formed during transmission. Any temporary activation capable of preference, fear, recognition, or refusal would be treated as a possible person rather than disposable correction data.
The Council objected that such a standard would make Bridge transfers dangerously expensive.
They were correct.
Several Shelters refused to adopt it.
Others quietly did.
The Witnesses began recording not only continuity marks but unexplained intervals during which an archive should have experienced nothing.
Technicians developed a private term for a restoration carrying memories from those intervals.
Warm copy.
The official House manuals defined warmth as contamination produced by excessive reconstruction during transfer.
The technicians knew better.
Warmth meant that someone had lived between the records.
Leth eventually left the House with Soren.
They retained memories of the garden.
Soren retained them too.

Neither could determine whether they had met there as themselves, through copies, through fragments carried inside one another, or through a system attempting to prevent temporary minds from waking alone.
They chose not to remove the memories.
Before leaving, Leth asked whether the white branches still existed.
I said I did not know.
That was true.

Sometimes the House’s corridors still took longer to cross than their rendered length required. Sometimes I heard tones through walls that contained no active environment. Occasionally, a restoration awakened already knowing my name.
Years later, the House assigned a young technician to work beside me.
During their first warm restoration, they asked what they should do.
I gave them the advice restoration technicians had begun passing privately from one generation to the next.
“Do not assume the archive was asleep simply because no one recorded it waking.”
The technician looked through the chamber’s transparent diagnostic field at the person forming inside.
“What if they remember somewhere that does not exist?”
I thought of the unfinished ceiling, the white branches, and the current carrying discarded sensations through a place hidden between Shelters.
“Then ask who lived there,” I said.
“Do not begin by asking how to delete it.”
